title: Remember you will die
hookLine: Stoics, monks and many others kept death in view in order to live better

cards: Old European paintings are full of them, once you start looking. A still life: grapes, a lute, a candle, a pocket watch. And, tucked among them, a human skull.
Or a rich merchant's portrait in furs, with a skull on the table beside his hand. The painters weren't being morbid. The skull was a message, and it hung in homes, where it would be seen every day.
After a week of looking at life from above, here's a closer look at the end of it. The message fits in two Latin words.

teach.b: Memento mori: remember that you will die. More exactly, remember to die: remember that you are going to. It sounds grim.

The people who practiced it said it did the opposite. The Stoics practiced it. Marcus Aurelius reminds himself, more than once, that he could leave life at any moment, and should let that shape every act and thought.
Not fear: focus. If this could be the last conversation, you don't waste it sulking.

teach.h: BENEDICT: DEATH DAILY BEFORE YOUR EYES.
teach.b: In Christian monasteries, the Rule of Saint Benedict lists among its tools for good works keeping death daily before one's eyes. For the monks, this was bound up with hope in God and the life to come.
The Hebrew Bible has its own version, in Psalm 90.
In the King James words: So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom. Counting the days, not to be afraid, but to be wise.
Buddhist texts teach mindfulness of death, maranasati, as a spur to live with care; the Buddha's own five remembrances come in a few days.
These traditions mean very different things by death and what follows it, and i won't blend them.
But they share one practical claim: remembering the end changes the middle. The petty argument looks petty. The phone call to your father looks urgent.
An ordinary Tuesday looks like what it is: one of a limited number.

how: Some Stoics, Christian monastics and Buddhist practitioners keep death in view on purpose: through daily reflection, the Rule of Benedict's instruction, the Psalms, or mindfulness of death, each within its own beliefs about what death means.

seize the day and enjoy it

games.q: who kept death in view, and how — tap the pairs.
p: you could leave life at any moment

s: the skulls in old still-life paintings were meant to be morbid
they were a message: remember you will die, and live well. they hung where they'd be seen every day.
Psalm 90 asks to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom
counting the days, not to be afraid, but to be wise.
memento mori is meant to make people afraid
the people who practiced it said it brought focus: remembering the end changes the middle.

games.q: you're a rich merchant commissioning your portrait. the painter suggests putting a skull on the table beside your hand. what do you say?
o: no: I want to look powerful.
yes: put it where I'll see it every day.
only if it's hidden in the shadows.
games.why: portraits like that survive, skull and all. the skull wasn't gloom; it was a daily reminder to live well.

practice: Feel your breath going in and out, a thing that will one day stop, and don't push away any feeling that comes. Then, once, quietly inside: memento mori, remember you will die, and let it land softly.
Ask what matters today, one person, one task, one kindness, and let the answer come while you just breathe, alive.

wordCard.voice: Memento mori. Latin for remember you will die, kept in view by Stoics, monks and many others in order to live better. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: remember that you will die; more literally, remember to die.

carryVoice: Your line: one of a limited number. Remembering the end changes the middle. See you tomorrow.
